title: IF SEX BETWEEN HUSBAND AND WIFE MADE THEM “UNCLEAN”… THEN WHAT HAVE WE BEEN GETTING WRONG ABOUT UNCLEANNESS?
paragraphs: IF SEX BETWEEN HUSBAND AND WIFE MADE THEM “UNCLEAN”… THEN WHAT HAVE WE BEEN GETTING WRONG ABOUT UNCLEANNESS?
Leviticus 15:18 may destroy one of our most damaging assumptions about holiness: that everything Scripture calls “unclean” must therefore be morally sinful, shameful, dirty, or disgusting.
There is a verse in Leviticus that almost nobody puts on a coffee mug.
Nobody cross-stitches it above the fireplace.
Nobody chooses it for the wedding ceremony.
And yet it may rescue someone who has spent years believing that God looks at human weakness, bodily existence, sexuality, sickness, blood, grief, or brokenness with disgust.
Listen carefully.
The Hebrew text of Leviticus 15:18 says:
וְאִשָּׁה אֲשֶׁר יִשְׁכַּב אִישׁ אֹתָהּ שִׁכְבַת־זָרַע וְרָחֲצוּ בַמַּיִם וְטָמְאוּ עַד־הָעָרֶב
Ve’ishshah asher yishkav ish otah shikhvat-zara, verachatsu vamayim, vetam’u ad-ha‘arev.
In straightforward English:
When a man has sexual relations with a woman involving an emission of semen, they are to wash themselves with water, and they remain ritually unclean until evening.
Both of them.
Unclean.
Until evening.
And that should make you stop.
Because if you have unconsciously been reading the biblical word “unclean” as another word for “sinful,” something immediately becomes difficult.
God created marriage.
God created the human body.
God created sexual union within the covenant boundaries He established.
Genesis presents the husband and wife becoming “one flesh.”
Yet Leviticus 15:18 says that intercourse involving semen results in a temporary state of uncleanness.
So either marital intimacy itself was morally sinful—which Scripture does not teach—or we have been forcing the word “unclean” to carry a meaning it does not always carry.
That changes more than one verse.
It changes how you read entire sections of your Bible.
The Hebrew word behind this language comes from טָמֵא — tame’, meaning to be unclean or impure in the ritual sense appropriate to these laws.
And here is the distinction many Christians were never taught:
Ritual impurity and moral guilt are not identical categories.
Sometimes they intersect.
But they cannot simply be collapsed into one another.
Leviticus 15 itself makes that extraordinarily difficult to deny.

Just two verses earlier, a man who has an emission of semen must wash his body and remains unclean until evening. Clothing or leather touched by the semen must likewise be washed and remains unclean until evening.
Then comes verse 18.
Sexual intercourse.
Wash.
Unclean until evening.
Notice what is missing.
No command to repent.
No declaration that the couple has committed adultery.
No moral condemnation of the intercourse itself.
No punishment.
No instruction to bring restitution because one spouse sinned against the other.
The text describes a ritual condition requiring purification and the passage of time.
That is not the same thing as saying sin does not matter.
It means precisely the opposite:
We must allow Scripture to define sin instead of making every biblical category mean “sin.”
This becomes even clearer when you notice what else could produce ritual impurity in the Torah.
Childbirth could.
Menstruation could.
Certain bodily discharges could.
Contact with a corpse could.
And ordinary seminal emission could.
These are not one moral category.
A woman giving birth has not committed a moral crime by giving birth.
A person does not become morally wicked because someone they love died and they encountered death.
A normal bodily emission is not automatically an act of rebellion against God.
The biblical world contains categories that many modern readers have flattened into a single word:
dirty.
And once we do that, something terrible happens.
We begin attaching shame where God did not attach shame.
Maybe somebody needs to hear that tonight.
Because some people have spent their entire Christian lives confusing human frailty with moral rebellion.
You felt something in your body and immediately thought God was disgusted.
You experienced something embarrassing and assumed heaven stepped backward.
You went through sickness and secretly wondered whether God was punishing you.
You carried wounds from sexual abuse and somehow absorbed the shame of what somebody else did to you.
You struggled with bodily realities nobody in church wanted to discuss, so silence taught you what Scripture never did:
Your body is dirty.
But the Bible's categories are more careful than that.
And God is more careful with wounded people than many wounded people have learned to be with themselves.
Leviticus does not teach that impurity was meaningless. Far from it.
Israel lived with the astonishing reality that the holy God had placed His dwelling among them.
Leviticus 15 eventually explains the seriousness of these regulations in relation to God's sanctuary. Ritual impurity had to be managed because Israel lived around sacred space.
That means tame’ was real.
But real does not automatically mean morally culpable.
That distinction matters.
A person could enter an impure condition through an ordinary biological process and later return to ritual cleanness through the procedure God prescribed.
This is why Leviticus 15:18 is so revealing.
A husband and wife could engage in legitimate sexual intimacy and nevertheless become ritually unclean until evening.
If unclean always meant sinful, the verse would create an enormous theological problem.
But once we stop forcing ritual impurity and moral evil into the same box, the problem begins to disappear.
And suddenly another truth becomes visible.
God is not embarrassed by the human body.
We are.
God speaks about blood.
Semen.
Discharges.
Menstruation.
Childbirth.
Sex.
Disease.
Death.
Things religious people sometimes whisper about, Scripture speaks about without blushing.
The Bible is astonishingly honest about what it means to live inside mortal flesh.
And perhaps that honesty is itself part of the lesson.
Because humanity's deepest problem was never that human beings possessed bodies.
Our deepest problem was sin.
There is a difference.
The human body was God's idea before sin ever entered Eden.
Male and female were God's idea.
Marriage was God's idea.
The one-flesh union was God's idea.
And before Genesis ever describes humanity's rebellion, Scripture says something breathtaking about God's creation:
“very good.”
Sin corrupted God's world.
Sin distorted sexuality.
Sin weaponized desire.
Sin introduced exploitation, adultery, lust, violence, selfishness, betrayal, and shame.
But Christianity does not teach that matter itself is evil.
Jesus Christ Himself came in flesh.
Think about that.
The eternal Son did not save humanity by refusing to touch humanity.
He entered it.
He was conceived.
Born.
Held.
Fed.
He became tired.
He slept.
He wept.
He bled.
He touched people other people avoided.
And then something extraordinary begins happening in the Gospel accounts.
Jesus touches the unclean.
Yet instead of uncleanness defeating Him…
His holiness overwhelms what is broken.
A leper approaches Jesus.
In the ancient world, people backed away.
Jesus reaches forward.
He touches him.
And the man becomes clean.
Then there is the woman whose story echoes the world of Leviticus 15 with almost painful precision.
She has suffered from bleeding for twelve years.
Twelve years.
Try not to read that as a statistic.
Imagine waking up tomorrow with the same problem you had yesterday.
Then imagine doing it for twelve years.
Mark tells us she had suffered terribly, spent what she had, and rather than improving, became worse.
She enters the crowd.
She reaches toward Jesus.
She touches His garment.
And the bleeding stops.
Do you see the reversal?
She comes carrying a condition associated with impurity.
She touches Jesus.
And Jesus does not become corrupted.
She becomes healed.
That is the kind of Savior standing at the center of Christianity.
Not a Savior terrified that your brokenness might contaminate Him.
A Savior powerful enough to enter your brokenness and transform you.
And this is where Leviticus becomes far more beautiful than the stereotype that it is merely an ancient book of strange restrictions.
Leviticus teaches you something about holiness.
The Gospels show you holiness walking toward sinners with a human face.
His name is Jesus.
But there is another distinction we must guard carefully.
Understanding ritual impurity does not mean pretending moral sin no longer exists.
Jesus did not erase the difference between good and evil.
He intensified the confrontation with evil by taking it all the way into the human heart.
He taught that what proceeds from within—from the heart—includes sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, greed, deceit, pride, and other evils, and that these things truly defile a person.
That is moral defilement.
So Christianity does not say:
“Nothing is unclean anymore, therefore nothing is sinful.”
It says something far more searching.
You cannot measure holiness merely by external conditions while ignoring the rebellion living inside the heart.
A person can look religious and harbor hatred.
A person can appear clean and secretly exploit others.
A person can quote Scripture and commit adultery.
A person can obsess over external purity while being eaten alive by pride.
Jesus repeatedly dragged religion back toward the heart.
And suddenly the question becomes uncomfortable.
What if you have been ashamed of things that were never your sin…
while excusing things that actually are?
What if you hate your body but tolerate your bitterness?
What if you are ashamed of weakness but proud of unforgiveness?
What if you hide scars you never chose while protecting sins you repeatedly choose?
That is where this stops being an interesting Bible study.
Now it is standing in your living room.
Now it knows your name.
Because there are people reading this who need freedom from false shame.
And there are other people reading this who need repentance from real sin.
Sometimes it is the same person.
Maybe you.
Maybe me.
Maybe all of us in different places.
Some things happened to you.
Other things were done by you.
Wisdom knows the difference.
Grace can meet you in both places, but grace meets them differently.
Jesus does not command you to repent for being wounded.
But He does call you to repent where you have sinned.
He does not condemn you for another person's violence against you.
But He will confront the bitterness, hatred, lust, deception, pride, or rebellion you choose to nurture.
That is what makes the Gospel so devastatingly beautiful.
Jesus neither invents guilt where there is none…
nor pretends guilt does not exist where it does.
He tells the truth.
Then He carries sinners toward mercy.
Maybe this is why some of us have misunderstood holiness.
We thought holiness meant never having anything messy near us.
Jesus showed holiness walking directly into the mess.
We thought holiness meant appearing untouched.
Jesus touched lepers.
We thought holiness meant hiding scars.
Jesus rose from the grave still bearing wounds.
And we thought salvation meant becoming impressive enough that God would finally tolerate us.
Then the cross destroyed the illusion.
Christianity begins with the humiliating confession that we could not rescue ourselves.
The Son of God had to come for us.
The scandal of the Gospel is not that sinners eventually became good enough to climb toward God.
The scandal is that God came down.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ bore judgment.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose.
And forgiveness is offered not because we successfully washed ourselves into acceptability, but because Jesus accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
Water could wash ritual impurity from skin.
But water cannot wash hatred from the heart.
Time could bring an Israelite to evening.
But time cannot atone for adultery.
A bath cannot erase greed.
A religious ceremony cannot crucify pride.
Something deeper was necessary.
Someone was necessary.
Jesus.
This is why Christians must be careful when moving from Leviticus to Christ.
The point is not that Leviticus was primitive nonsense that Jesus discarded.

The point is that Israel's purity system belonged to a covenantal world centered around God's holy presence among His people, teaching distinctions between holy and common, clean and unclean, and regulating access to sacred space.
Then Christ comes.
And everything converges on Him.
He is not merely another teacher standing outside the system giving commentary.
He is the Holy One.
The sacrifice.
The priestly mediator.
The One through whom sinners approach God.
And Hebrews gives Christians language that would have sounded almost shocking against the background we have been discussing:
Marriage is to be honored, and the marriage bed is to remain undefiled; God judges sexual immorality and adultery.
There it is again.
Sex is not automatically dirty.
But sex can be corrupted by sin.
Marriage does not sanctify every conceivable behavior merely because married people perform it, nor does Scripture treat marital intimacy itself as shameful.
Biblical holiness refuses both errors.
It refuses the culture that turns sex into a god.
And it refuses the religious shame that treats sex within God's design as inherently filthy.
God's answer is covenant.
Faithfulness.
Love.
Self-giving.
Holiness.
Honor.
And this distinction may matter far beyond sexuality.
Because perhaps you have been calling yourself unclean when what you really are is wounded.
Perhaps you have been calling yourself condemned when what you really need is healing.
Perhaps somebody else's sin became your shame.
Perhaps something happened to you when you were young and you have carried the invisible accusation ever since:
Dirty.
Hear this carefully.
What somebody did against you is not automatically your moral guilt.
Jesus knows the difference between the sinner and the sinned-against.
He knows where responsibility belongs.
He knows what was chosen and what was forced.
He knows what you did and what was done to you.
He knows every hidden room in the story.
And nobody has to deceive Him to receive mercy.
You can tell Him the truth.
All of it.
The part that hurts.
The part that embarrasses you.
The part you regret.
The part that was not your fault.
The part that absolutely was.
Bring the entire scandal into the light.
Because Jesus does something astonishing with scandals surrendered to Him.
He writes grace into places where shame thought it would have the final sentence.
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
It does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
Grace is not God's permission to remain enslaved to sin.
Grace is God's invitation to come out of hiding.
To confess.
To repent.
To receive forgiveness.
To walk differently.
To become new.
Maybe the most dangerous lie shame ever taught you was:
“If Jesus knew everything, He wouldn't want me.”
But Jesus already knows everything.
The cross happened anyway.
The invitation still stands.
So stop confusing your scars with your sins.
And stop renaming your sins as scars so you can avoid repentance.
Bring both to Jesus.
Let Him heal what was done to you.
Let Him forgive what was done by you.
Let Him expose what needs exposing.
Let Him cleanse what truly defiles.
Let Him restore what shame told you could never be restored.
If this exposed something you have hidden for years, you do not have to write your whole story publicly. But you can take one small step out of hiding.
And when you see someone else write those words, do not interrogate them.
Pray for them.
Somebody behind that screen may be fighting a battle you know nothing about.
And yes—even send it to the skeptic who believes Christianity has nothing intelligent or compassionate to say about the body.
Let Scripture speak for itself.
The mission is simple: daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
It cannot.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior replaces generosity to your local church, care for the poor, or other forms of Christian giving.
It does not.

But Scripture does teach voluntary, willing, generous support of Gospel work. If Gospel Warrior is one of the ministries spiritually feeding you, you can choose to make supporting this work part of your regular Christian giving—an offering given freely before God, not a payment extracted through guilt.
That costs nothing.
A single share can put the Gospel in front of someone we could never reach ourselves.
One share can enter a hospital room.
A broken marriage.
A teenager's midnight scroll.
A believer quietly drowning in shame.
A skeptic asking questions nobody knows they are asking.
We may never know this side of eternity what God does with one faithful click offered for His glory.
So comment.
Save.
Share.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody still thinks unclean means unlovable.
Somebody still thinks their scar is their identity.
Somebody still believes their worst chapter gets the final word.
And somebody desperately needs to discover what the Gospel has been saying all along:
Jesus is not frightened by the chapter you are ashamed to show Him.
Bring Him the page you thought ruined your story—and watch what happens when the pen is placed in the hands of Grace.
